query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A novel hybrid computational method that integrates DFT‐guided machine learning potentials with Boltzmann transport analysis can decouple lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr by explicitly accounting for atomic‐scale disorder (including defect scattering such as 1 wt.% oxygen contamination) and will yield conductivity predictions with a reduced error margin (approximately 20–30% improvement) compared to traditional approaches based on perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr alloy, considering both an ideal defect‐free state and a realistic state with atomic‐scale disorder (including oxygen at roughly 1 wt.%).
generation.intervention: Application of the hybrid computational method that combines DFT-guided machine-learned interatomic potentials with Boltzmann transport analysis to separately model phonon (lattice) and electron contributions.
generation.conditions: Evaluations performed across a temperature range from below 200 K (where experimental observations indicate comparable lattice and electronic contributions) up to 1200 K (covering total conductivity measurements in the 10–17 W/(K·m) range), including testing on samples with controlled oxygen contamination.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale disorder and defects (such as vacancies, substitutional disorder, and oxygen impurities) that alter local bonding environments and scattering mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly simulating defect-induced lattice distortions and local environmental variations, the method decouples phonon and electron transport channels. This enables more accurate Boltzmann transport calculations by directly modeling the scattering events affecting each contribution.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model is expected to yield separate predictions for lattice and electronic thermal conductivity that match experimental trends—exhibiting lower overall prediction errors (improved by about 20–30% compared to approaches relying on Debye temperature estimates for perfect crystals) and showing that below 200 K the two contributions are comparable while at higher temperatures the total conductivity remains in the 10–17 W/(K·m) range in oxygen-contaminated samples.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical and simulation approaches that assume perfect, defect-free bulk crystals and that conflate lattice and electronic contributions using Debye temperature-based estimates.
generation.boundary: The method’s predictive accuracy is expected to be robust for samples where defect characteristics (including up to 1 wt.% oxygen) are well characterized in the simulation; however, predictions may be less reliable at temperatures above 1200 K or under conditions with unmodeled extreme non-equilibrium or excessive defect concentrations.
generation.uncertainty: While the estimated improvement is about 20–30%, exact numerical precision is uncertain due to potential variability in defect modeling and the challenges inherent in fully decoupling electron and phonon transport channels under all conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled oxygen contamination and measure the separate components of thermal conductivity (lattice vs. electronic) across a temperature range from below 200 K to 1200 K using independent experimental techniques.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity via phonon spectroscopy or thermal diffusivity methods
Electronic thermal conductivity inferred from electrical resistivity measurements using the Wiedemann-Franz relation
Total thermal conductivity for cross-validation of the decoupling strategy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured separate conductivity components do not align with the predictions (e.g., if the improvement in prediction error is significantly less than 20–30% or if the temperature-dependent trends do not match), then the hypothesis that the new method accurately decouples and predicts lattice and electronic contributions will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. We demonstrate that the impact of this inter-atomic length disorder (representing static lattice distortion) and temperature fluctuations (representing dynamic lattice distortion) on fundamental and universal thermodynamic, structural, and elastic characteristics are similar and can be unified through effective temperature; i.e. a scaling law for HEAs that establishes a relationship between these factors. Recently, PbSnTeSe has been experimentally investigated by Fan et al. [] and Raphel et al. [,], who report appreciably similar results for the thermoelectric performance of the material (see below). The modelling of HEAs transport properties constitute a challenge, and both the simulation methods and their derived predictions have to be confronted to experimental data to assess their validity. In this context, we present in this paper for the first time a complete approach that allows one to obtain all the transport coefficients, including the figure of merit, of a high-entropy alloy. The thermoelectric transport properties of the PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloy have been calculated by combining state-of-the-art methods based on the special quasi-random structures approach to generate the HEA structure, the first-principles density-functional theory (DFT), and the Boltzmann transport and Green–Kubo theories. First, from the DFT-computed material electronic states, the electronic transport properties (electronic conductivity, Seebeck coefficient and electronic thermal conductivity) were calculated using the linearized Boltzmann transport equation, and the power factor was obtained.
